segments.title: Predict: front insertion versus append
segments.description:
Show a Python list of 200,000 integers. Pose the question: which is faster, 1,000 calls to insert at position 0 or 1,000 calls to append?
Each student writes a prediction and a rough ratio, then compares with a partner for one minute.
Run the timing live and hear two predictions against the result.
segments.teacherNotes:
Timings vary by machine, so quote only what the screen shows. Expect the front insertions to be much slower. Name the cause only as a question to answer next. Run this code live:
`import time`
`n = 200_000`
`lst = list(range(n))`
`start = time.perf_counter()`
`for _ in range(1000):`
`    lst.insert(0, -1)`
`print(time.perf_counter() - start)`
`lst = list(range(n))`
`start = time.perf_counter()`
`for _ in range(1000):`
`    lst.append(-1)`
`print(time.perf_counter() - start)`
shown: A list holds 200,000 integers. Which is faster: 1,000 calls to lst.insert(0, -1), or 1,000 calls to lst.append(-1)? Write your guess and about how many times faster.

segments.title: How a Python list is stored
segments.description:
Draw a list as one contiguous block of references. Item i sits at the base address plus i times the size of one reference, so indexing is O(1).
Show that inserting at index i moves every item from i onward one slot right, which is n − i moves. Deleting moves them left.
Students predict, then check on the drawing: how many items move when 99 is inserted at the front of an 8-item list, and at the end?
segments.teacherNotes: Answer: 8 moves at the front, 0 at the end. Misconception: Python’s list is a dynamic array, not a linked list, despite the name. Stress that the array holds references, not the objects themselves.

segments.title: Building a singly linked list
segments.description:
Write Node and LinkedList on screen line by line, drawing each node as a box with an arrow to the next. Cover insert_front, append and search.
Before running append, students trace on paper the list 4 → 8 → 15 after append(16). They state how many times `cur = cur.next` runs.
State the costs: insert_front is O(1), while append (head pointer only) and search are O(n).
segments.teacherNotes:
Answer: 2 hops. Point out `next` shadows a built-in name here, harmless in this class. Full code:
`class Node:`
`    def __init__(self, value, next=None):`
`        self.value = value`
`        self.next = next`
`class LinkedList:`
`    def __init__(self):`
`        self.head = None`
`    def insert_front(self, value):`
`        self.head = Node(value, self.head)`
`    def append(self, value):`
`        node = Node(value)`
`        if self.head is None:`
`            self.head = node`
`            return`
`        cur = self.head`
`        while cur.next is not None:`
`            cur = cur.next`
`        cur.next = node`
`    def search(self, value):`
`        cur = self.head`
`        while cur is not None:`
`            if cur.value == value:`
`                return True`
`            cur = cur.next`
`        return False`
Then run this example, which builds 4 → 8 → 15, appends 16 and prints 4, 8, 15, 16, one per line:
`lst = LinkedList()`
`for v in (15, 8, 4):`
`    lst.insert_front(v)`
`lst.append(16)`
`cur = lst.head`
`while cur is not None:`
`    print(cur.value)`
`    cur = cur.next`

segments.title: Write delete
segments.description:
Each student writes delete(value) for LinkedList alone for six minutes. It removes the first node holding value and returns True, or returns False if none holds it.
Pairs then test it on the list 3 → 5 → 7 by deleting 3, then 7, then 9, and compare code.
segments.teacherNotes:
Common mistake: forgetting that deleting the head must change self.head. Expected results: delete(3) True, delete(7) True, delete(9) False. Sample solution:
`def delete(self, value):`
`    prev = None`
`    cur = self.head`
`    while cur is not None:`
`        if cur.value == value:`
`            if prev is None:`
`                self.head = cur.next`
`            else:`
`                prev.next = cur.next`
`            return True`
`        prev = cur`
`        cur = cur.next`
`    return False`

segments.title: Why append is amortized O(1)
segments.description:
Explain the model: a full array allocates a new one of double the capacity and copies every item, which is O(n) for that one append.
Students compute the copies made over 16 appends into a list that starts at capacity 1. They add the 16 writes and divide by 16.
State the conclusion: the average cost per append stays bounded by a constant, so append is amortized O(1).
segments.teacherNotes: Answer: resizes copy 1+2+4+8 = 15 items; total work 16 + 15 = 31, under 2 per append. CPython actually over-allocates by a smaller factor, roughly 1.125, and the argument still holds. Misconception: amortized does not mean average over random inputs.

segments.title: Find and fix the mistake in insert_at
segments.description:
Show a method meant to insert value at position index of a LinkedList, with the list 2 → 6 → 9 and 0 ≤ index ≤ the length of the list.
Students work alone on paper for six minutes: run insert_at(1, 4) and write the list it gives, name the line or lines responsible, write the corrected lines, then trace the fixed method on insert_at(0, 4).
Pairs compare fixes for two minutes. Hear one pair’s explanation.
segments.teacherNotes:
Bug: both `node = Node(value)` lines never set the new node’s next, so the rest of the list is lost. Before the fix, insert_at(1, 4) gives 2 → 4. After the fix, insert_at(1, 4) gives 2 → 4 → 6 → 9 and insert_at(0, 4) gives 4 → 2 → 6 → 9. Fixed lines:
`node = Node(value, self.head)`
`node = Node(value, cur.next)`

keyIdeas: A Python list stores references in one contiguous array. Indexing is O(1), but inserting or deleting at the front or middle shifts items, which costs O(n).
A singly linked list chains nodes through next references. Inserting at the head is O(1), but reaching position i or searching by value needs an O(n) traversal.
list.append is amortized O(1): an occasional resize copies every item, but those copies are spread over many cheap appends.
No structure wins on every operation. Choose by the mix of operations a program performs most.

vocabulary.definition: A resizable array that holds items in one contiguous block of memory. Python’s list is implemented this way.
The number of slots allocated in an array, which can exceed the number of items currently stored.
An object in a linked list that holds a value and a reference to the next node.
The reference to the first node of a linked list. It is None when the list is empty.
Visiting nodes one after another by following next references, as search and append do.
A cost that does not grow with the number of items n.
A cost that grows in proportion to the number of items n.
The cost per operation averaged over a whole sequence of operations, so a rare expensive step is spread across many cheap ones.

study.overview: A Python list and a singly linked list can hold the same values, but they store them differently, so the same operation costs different amounts. A Python list keeps references side by side in one array. A linked list chains separate nodes together with next references. This guide covers how each structure is laid out, what that costs for indexing, insertion, deletion, search and append, why list.append is still amortized O(1), and how to choose between the two. For optional further reading, see Goodrich, Tamassia & Goldwasser (2013), Data Structures and Algorithms in Python, ch. 7 (to confirm).

points.heading: A Python list is a contiguous array of references
points.explanation:
A Python list stores references to its items in one contiguous block of memory. Item i sits at the base address plus i times the size of one reference, so the program jumps straight to it. Indexing is O(1). The array holds references, not the objects themselves, and despite its name a Python list is not a linked list.

The cost appears when you insert or delete away from the end. Inserting at index i moves every item from i onward one slot to the right, which is n − i moves. Deleting moves them one slot to the left.

Example: take an 8-item list and insert 99 at the front. All 8 items shift right, so there are 8 moves. Insert 99 at the end instead and nothing shifts, so there are 0 moves. This is why 1,000 calls to `lst.insert(0, -1)` on a list of 200,000 integers run much slower than 1,000 calls to `lst.append(-1)`. Each front insertion shifts every item, and each append does not.

points.heading: A singly linked list trades fast indexing for cheap front insertion
points.explanation:
A singly linked list is a chain of nodes. Each node holds a value and a next reference, and the list keeps only a head pointer to the first node. Here is the code from class:

`class Node:`
`    def __init__(self, value, next=None):`
`        self.value = value`
`        self.next = next`
`class LinkedList:`
`    def __init__(self):`
`        self.head = None`
`    def insert_front(self, value):`
`        self.head = Node(value, self.head)`
`    def append(self, value):`
`        node = Node(value)`
`        if self.head is None:`
`            self.head = node`
`            return`
`        cur = self.head`
`        while cur.next is not None:`
`            cur = cur.next`
`        cur.next = node`
`    def search(self, value):`
`        cur = self.head`
`        while cur is not None:`
`            if cur.value == value:`
`                return True`
`            cur = cur.next`
`        return False`

The name `next` shadows a built-in here, which is harmless in this class. `insert_front` creates one node and moves the head, so it is O(1). Nothing is shifted. Reaching position i, searching by value, and appending with only a head pointer all need a traversal from the head, so they are O(n).

Example: the list is 4 → 8 → 15 and you call `append(16)`. The loop starts at the node holding 4 and runs `cur = cur.next` twice, stopping at the node holding 15, whose next is None. That node’s next is then set to the new node, giving 4 → 8 → 15 → 16.

Deletion follows the same pattern. Walk the list while remembering the previous node, then make the previous node’s next skip the target. If the target is the first node, there is no previous node, so you must change `self.head` instead. Forgetting this case is a common mistake. Likewise, when you insert a node in the middle, set its next to the rest of the list before you link it in, or the remaining nodes are lost.

points.heading: Why list.append is amortized O(1)
points.explanation:
A Python list sits in an array of fixed capacity. When an append finds the array full, Python allocates a larger array and copies every item across. That one append costs O(n). But resizes are rare, and each one makes room for many cheap appends afterward.

Example: use a simple model in which capacity starts at 1 and doubles whenever the array is full. Over 16 appends the resizes copy 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15 items. Add the 16 writes of the new values and the total work is 16 + 15 = 31. Divided by 16 appends, that is under 2 units of work per append. The average stays below a constant however long the sequence grows.

That is what amortized O(1) means: the cost per append, averaged over a whole sequence of appends, is bounded by a constant, even though a single append can be expensive. It is not an average over random inputs. It is a guarantee about the total cost of any sequence of appends. CPython actually grows the array by a smaller factor, roughly 1.125, and the argument still holds.

points.heading: Choose a structure by its operation mix
points.explanation:
Neither structure wins on every operation. Compare them, with the linked list having a head pointer only and n items:

Get item at index i: Python list O(1), linked list O(n).
Insert at front: Python list O(n), linked list O(1).
Append: Python list amortized O(1), linked list O(n).

Searching by value is O(n) in both, because either one may have to examine every item. A tail pointer would make linked-list append O(1), which shows how the answer depends on what the structure keeps track of.

To choose, look at what the program does most often. Suppose a program reads the item at a given position thousands of times and only occasionally adds to the end. The Python list fits, because indexing is O(1) and append is amortized O(1). Suppose instead a program keeps adding items at the head and walks the whole collection from the start each time it reads. A linked list fits, because front insertion is O(1) and walking from the head is the access it needs anyway.

handouts.title: Write delete for LinkedList

blocks.text: Work alone first. Below is the code from class. Type it into your editor, then add a method delete(value) to LinkedList. It removes the first node holding value and returns True. If no node holds value, it returns False.

blocks.hint: Write the method as it would sit inside LinkedList, starting with its def line.

blocks.text: Add your method to the class, then run this code. The three delete calls run one after another on the same list.

blocks.hint: If your result differs from your partner's, note which lines of the two methods differ.

handouts.key:
Your delete method

One correct implementation, indented to sit inside LinkedList:

- `    def delete(self, value):`
- `        prev = None`
- `        cur = self.head`
- `        while cur is not None:`
- `            if cur.value == value:`
- `                if prev is None:`
- `                    self.head = cur.next`
- `                else:`
- `                    prev.next = cur.next`
- `                return True`
- `            prev = cur`
- `            cur = cur.next`
- `        return False`

Look for traversal from the head, removal of only the first matching node, preservation of the remaining links, and the required Boolean return value. Accept equivalent implementations. An empty list returns False. Deleting the head must update self.head. Common slips are leaving self.head unchanged, losing the nodes after the deleted node, removing every match, or returning False before the traversal finishes.

Test with your partner

| Call | Printed |
| --- | --- |
| `lst.delete(3)` | True |
| `lst.delete(7)` | True |
| `lst.delete(9)` | False |

The starting list is 3 → 5 → 7. Deleting 3 leaves 5 → 7. Deleting 7 then leaves 5. Searching for 9 reaches the end without a match, so the list remains 5. Common slip: treating each call as if it starts with the original list.

Comparison of methods

If results differ, look for identification of the differing lines and an explanation of how they affect the head, traversal, links, or return value. Correct methods may use different code and still produce the same results. If results agree, no discrepancy needs to be recorded.

handouts.title: Find and fix the mistake in insert_at
handouts.usedIn: Find and fix the mistake in insert_at

blocks.text: The method below is meant to insert value at position index in a LinkedList, so that the new node ends up at that position. Assume 0 ≤ index ≤ the length of the list. It uses the Node and LinkedList classes from class. Work on paper.
The list is 2 → 6 → 9, with head pointing at the node holding 2.

items: Run insert_at(1, 4) on paper. Write the list you get, starting from the head.
What goes wrong? Name the line or lines responsible.
Trace your fixed method on insert_at(0, 4) for the same list. Write the list you get.

blocks.hint: Your corrected lines, with the line they replace.
Your trace of insert_at(0, 4) after the fix.

handouts.key:
Trace of insert_at(1, 4)

The index is not 0. cur starts at the node holding 2. The loop runs zero times because index − 1 = 0. The new node holds 4 and has next set to None. Assigning cur.next to that node gives 2 → 4 from the head.

What goes wrong, and where

Both occurrences of `node = Node(value)` create a node whose next is None. In the index-0 branch, replacing self.head loses the link to the original head. In the other branch, replacing cur.next loses the link to the original successor. Look for both branches in the answer. Common slip: identifying only the assignment to cur.next, without explaining that the new node must retain the old successor.

Corrected lines

Replace the node-creation line inside the index-0 branch with:

- `        node = Node(value, self.head)`

Replace the node-creation line after the loop with:

- `    node = Node(value, cur.next)`

Accept equivalent fixes that set node.next to the original head or successor before changing self.head or cur.next. Common slip: changing the head or successor first and then using that changed reference, creating a self-link.

Trace of insert_at(0, 4) after the fix

Start with 2 → 6 → 9. The new node holds 4 and points to the original head, which holds 2. self.head then points to the new node. The method returns, giving 4 → 2 → 6 → 9. Common slip: starting from the list changed by the earlier trace instead of the specified original list.

handouts.title: Cost comparison table

blocks.text: Fill in the running time of each operation in O notation, in terms of n, the number of items. The linked list has a head pointer only, with no tail pointer.

handouts.key:
| Operation | Python list | Linked list (head pointer only) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Get item at index i | O(1) | O(n) |
| Insert at front | O(n) | O(1) |
| Append | Amortized O(1) | O(n) |

Use worst-case costs unless amortized cost is explicitly stated. Python list indexing directly accesses a reference. Linked list indexing traverses i links, giving O(i + 1), which is O(n) in the worst case. Front insertion into a Python list shifts n references; linked front insertion changes a constant number of references. Python list append occasionally resizes its array, so an individual append can take O(n), while append is amortized O(1). Linked append must traverse to the final node because there is no tail pointer.

Common slips: giving linked indexing O(1), treating every Python list append as worst-case O(1), or giving linked append O(1) despite the absence of a tail pointer.

segments.title: Stacks on a list and on linked nodes
segments.description:
Define a stack by push, pop, peek and is_empty. Write ListStack on screen, with the end of the list as the top.
Write LinkedStack beside it, reusing Node from last time, with the head as the top. Show that push is the head insertion students already know.
Each student writes what would go wrong if the list’s front were the top, then tells a partner.
segments.teacherNotes:
Answer: insert(0, x) and pop(0) shift every item, so each costs O(n), against amortized O(1) for push and O(1) for pop at the end. Peek is O(1) in both versions. Pop on an empty stack raises IndexError, as list.pop does. ListStack:
`class ListStack:`
`    def __init__(self):`
`        self._items = []`
`    def push(self, value):`
`        self._items.append(value)`
`    def pop(self):`
`        if not self._items:`
`            raise IndexError("pop from empty stack")`
`        return self._items.pop()`
`    def peek(self):`
`        if not self._items:`
`            raise IndexError("peek at empty stack")`
`        return self._items[-1]`
`    def is_empty(self):`
`        return not self._items`
LinkedStack:
`class LinkedStack:`
`    def __init__(self):`
`        self.head = None`
`    def push(self, value):`
`        self.head = Node(value, self.head)`
`    def peek(self):`
`        if self.head is None:`
`            raise IndexError("peek at empty stack")`
`        return self.head.value`
`    def is_empty(self):`
`        return self.head is None`
shown: Which end of a Python list is the top of ListStack? Which end of the chain is the top of LinkedStack?
If the top were the front of the list, what would go wrong, and what would push and pop cost?

segments.teacherNotes: Trace of {[()]}: stack grows to {, [, ( and empties in reverse order. For ([)]: stack is (, [ ; at ) the pop gives [, which does not match, so it fails at the third character. Do not show code yet.

segments.title: Find and fix the mistake in is_balanced
segments.description:
Show a classmate’s is_balanced that uses a list as a stack. Students run it on paper on three strings and write only the result for each: a value or an error.
Each student writes the fix alone for two minutes, in one or two lines. Partners compare fixes for one minute.
Hear one pair’s explanation, then show the corrected version.
segments.teacherNotes:
Expected: (() gives True, wrongly; )( crashes with IndexError from pop on an empty stack; ([)] correctly gives False. Fixes: test `not stack` before popping and return `not stack` at the end. Buggy:
`def is_balanced(text):`
`    pairs = {")": "(", "]": "[", "}": "{"}`
`    stack = []`
`    for ch in text:`
`        if ch in "([{":`
`            stack.append(ch)`
`        elif ch in pairs:`
`            if stack.pop() != pairs[ch]:`
`                return False`
`    return True`
Fixed:
`def is_balanced(text):`
`    pairs = {")": "(", "]": "[", "}": "{"}`
`    stack = []`
`    for ch in text:`
`        if ch in "([{":`
`            stack.append(ch)`
`        elif ch in pairs:`
`            if not stack or stack.pop() != pairs[ch]:`
`                return False`
`    return not stack`

study.overview: A stack and a queue both limit where items go in and where they come out. That limit is what makes them useful. A stack gives back the newest item first. A queue gives back the oldest item first. This guide covers how to build each one on a Python list and on linked nodes, how a stack checks that brackets are balanced, and why `collections.deque` is the right tool for a queue in Python. If you want a second explanation of these structures, Miller & Ranum (2011), Problem Solving with Algorithms and Data Structures Using Python, is optional further reading.

points.heading: A stack is last in, first out
points.explanation:
A stack has four operations: push adds an item, pop removes and returns the newest item, peek reads the newest item without removing it, and is_empty tests for no items. Push and pop both work at one end only, called the top. This order is last in, first out (LIFO).

Example: a stack starts empty and receives push(4), push(9), push(2). Then pop() returns 2, because 2 went in last. The stack now holds 4 and 9, with 9 on top.

On a Python list, make the end of the list the top. Push is `append`, which costs amortized O(1). Pop is `list.pop()`, which costs O(1). If the front of the list were the top, `insert(0, x)` and `pop(0)` would shift every item, so each would cost O(n). On linked nodes, make the head the top. Push is the head insertion from last time and pop moves head forward, so both cost O(1). Peek costs O(1) in both versions. Popping an empty stack raises IndexError, as `list.pop` does.

The linked version reuses this Node class:
`class Node:`
`    def __init__(self, value, next=None):`
`        self.value = value`
`        self.next = next`

Stack on a list:
`class ListStack:`
`    def __init__(self):`
`        self._items = []`
`    def push(self, value):`
`        self._items.append(value)`
`    def pop(self):`
`        if not self._items:`
`            raise IndexError("pop from empty stack")`
`        return self._items.pop()`
`    def peek(self):`
`        if not self._items:`
`            raise IndexError("peek at empty stack")`
`        return self._items[-1]`
`    def is_empty(self):`
`        return not self._items`

Stack on linked nodes:
`class LinkedStack:`
`    def __init__(self):`
`        self.head = None`
`    def push(self, value):`
`        self.head = Node(value, self.head)`
`    def pop(self):`
`        if self.head is None:`
`            raise IndexError("pop from empty stack")`
`        value = self.head.value`
`        self.head = self.head.next`
`        return value`
`    def peek(self):`
`        if self.head is None:`
`            raise IndexError("peek at empty stack")`
`        return self.head.value`
`    def is_empty(self):`
`        return self.head is None`

In `pop`, save the value before you move head. Return the value, not the node.

points.heading: Checking balanced parentheses with a stack
points.explanation:
The problem: decide whether every (, [ and { in a string is closed by the matching symbol, in the right order. A stack fits because the opener that must be closed first is always the most recent one still open.

The rule has three parts. Push each opener. On a closer, pop the top and compare it with the opener that closer needs. When the string ends, the stack must be empty.

Example that succeeds, {[()]}: the stack after each character is {, then { [, then { [ (. The ) pops ( and matches. The ] pops [ and matches. The } pops { and matches. The stack is empty, so the string is balanced.

Example that fails, ([)]: ( is pushed, then [ is pushed, so the stack is ( [ with [ on top. At the third character, ), the pop gives [, but ) needs (. The check fails at the third character, even though the counts of each symbol are equal. Order matters, not only counts.

Two more cases show why the rule has the empty checks:
- A closer arrives when the stack is empty, as in the string ]. There is nothing to pop. Test whether the stack is empty before you pop, and answer False if it is. Otherwise Python raises IndexError.
- Openers are left over at the end, as in {[]. Every closer matched, but { is still on the stack. Return True only if the stack is empty at the end.

When you write the function, use a dictionary that maps each closer to its opener, such as `{")": "(", "]": "[", "}": "{"}`. Then one comparison handles all three bracket types.

points.heading: Queues: why pop(0) is a poor dequeue
points.explanation:
A queue is first in, first out (FIFO). Enqueue adds at the back and dequeue removes from the front. Example: a queue starts empty and receives enqueue(4), enqueue(9), enqueue(2). Then dequeue() returns 4, because 4 arrived first.

The obvious list version appends at the back and removes at index 0:
`class ListQueue:`
`    def __init__(self):`
`        self._items = []`
`    def enqueue(self, value):`
`        self._items.append(value)`
`    def dequeue(self):`
`        if not self._items:`
`            raise IndexError("dequeue from empty queue")`
`        return self._items.pop(0)`
`    def is_empty(self):`
`        return not self._items`

Enqueue is amortized O(1). Dequeue is O(n), because `pop(0)` moves every remaining item one slot to the left.

A linked queue fixes this by keeping two references: head at the front and tail at the back. Dequeue moves head forward, which is O(1). Enqueue attaches a new node after tail, which is O(1) because you never walk the chain.
`class LinkedQueue:`
`    def __init__(self):`
`        self.head = None`
`        self.tail = None`
`    def enqueue(self, value):`
`        node = Node(value)`
`        if self.tail is None:`
`            self.head = node`
`        else:`
`            self.tail.next = node`
`        self.tail = node`
`    def dequeue(self):`
`        if self.head is None:`
`            raise IndexError("dequeue from empty queue")`
`        value = self.head.value`
`        self.head = self.head.next`
`        if self.head is None:`
`            self.tail = None`
`        return value`
`    def is_empty(self):`
`        return self.head is None`

There are two edge cases. When the queue is empty, enqueue must set head as well as tail. When the last node leaves, dequeue must set tail back to None. Otherwise tail still points at a node that is no longer in the queue. Check the code by enqueuing 2 and 4 on a new queue and then dequeuing once. The result is 2.

points.heading: Why collections.deque suits queues in Python
points.explanation:
A `collections.deque` gives O(1) append and O(1) pop at both ends. It is built from linked blocks, so `popleft` removes the front item without shifting the others. That matches the cost of the linked queue, without you writing the nodes. Use `append` to enqueue and `popleft` to dequeue.

The trade-off is indexing. Reaching an item in the middle of a deque is O(n), whereas a list indexes in O(1). A queue never needs the middle, so the trade costs nothing here.

You can see the difference by timing it. Each program removes 1000 items from the front of 200,000 items and prints the time in seconds. Run each in a fresh session.

Program A, a list:
`import time`
`n = 200_000`
`lst = list(range(n))`
`start = time.perf_counter()`
`for _ in range(1000):`
`    lst.pop(0)`
`print(time.perf_counter() - start)`

Program B, a deque:
`from collections import deque`
`import time`
`n = 200_000`
`dq = deque(range(n))`
`start = time.perf_counter()`
`for _ in range(1000):`
`    dq.popleft()`
`print(time.perf_counter() - start)`

Expect Program A to print a much larger time. Each `pop(0)` shifts about 200,000 references, and it does so 1000 times. Program B does constant work per removal. Run both yourself and compare with your own prediction.

Summary: use a list for a stack, with the end as the top. Use `collections.deque` for a queue. Write a linked queue with head and tail when you need to show how the O(1) costs arise.
